description: We’re building health monitoring software for astronauts: a tool that tracks vital signs, flags anomalies with machine learning, and helps crews act on their health status during long missions. Our skills: Python, ML, data analysis, embedded systems and app development. We’re open to new members, especially anyone with UI/UX, biomedical or health-data experience. Find us at the venue in Building S40!
summary:
ORBITAL is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support system for astronauts on long missions. It is built for crews who are not doctors and cannot count on help from Earth. On the way to Mars, messages take up to 22 minutes each way and evacuation is impossible for months, so the crew must notice and act on health changes themselves.

ORBITAL collects vital signs from an ESP32 sensor node (live heart rate), one-minute check-ins (sleep, mood, symptoms), quick tests and cabin readings. It compares each value with the astronaut's own preflight baseline and with NASA limits. Then it gives a colour-coded status, the reason in plain words, and the next step, including who should act: the astronaut, the Crew Medical Officer, or emergency steps. It reads body and cabin data together (for example, headaches + poor sleep + rising CO2). Real Inspiration4 crew lab data from NASA's Open Science Data Repository shows how values are read against each person's own baseline. ORBITAL supports decisions. It never diagnoses.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ORBITAL helps astronauts who are not medical professionals check their health, spot meaningful changes early, understand them, and take the right next step, even when Earth is minutes away or unreachable. It follows five steps: Collect, Assess, Explain, Guide, Follow up.

HOW IT WORKS

- Collect: live heart rate from an ESP32 node with a pulse sensor; SpO2 and blood pressure entered by hand; a guided check-in (sleep, mood, symptoms); two in-app tests, a 3-minute reaction-time test (PVT, the type of test NASA has flown on the ISS) and an Amsler-style vision grid for spaceflight-related vision changes (SANS); cabin temperature, humidity and CO2; radiation dose; and space-weather alerts from NASA DONKI.

- Assess: a deterministic rules engine compares each value with the astronaut's own preflight baseline (average and normal spread) and recent trend, and with cited limits, such as the NASA-STD-3001 cabin CO2 limit (3 mmHg, 1-hour average) and the 600 mSv career radiation limit. It also looks for combined patterns, such as recurring headaches + short sleep + rising CO2, and reports them as a "possible contributing factor", never a cause.

- Explain: every status shows its reason, tagged as cited, baseline or team rule, with the source. Each indicator has a card: what it is, why spaceflight affects it, what a result can and cannot mean, and how to measure it correctly, with common mistakes.

- Guide: each status level says who acts. Green: no action. Yellow: the astronaut (re-measure, self-care, re-test). Orange: the Crew Medical Officer reviews. Red: emergency steps.

- Follow up: cases, re-test reminders and a time-stamped log. A report packet goes to ground support with the real communication delay for the chosen mission profile (ISS, Moon or Mars, where the delay is 3 to 22 minutes one way). During a blackout, packets queue and are sent when the link returns, so the crew never waits for Earth.

- Ask: an offline assistant answers questions such as "how do I measure..." or "why does space affect...". It answers only from 15 short, cited documents written for the app, and shows its sources. It uses a small local AI model (Llama 3.2 3B through Ollama) when one is installed; otherwise it returns the best-matching passages. It refuses diagnosis, medication and dosing questions and points to the Crew Medical Officer. It never sets a status.

WHAT WE BUILT IN THE HACKATHON

- A web app that runs entirely on one laptop with no internet, started with one command. Other devices on the same network, such as a tablet for the medical officer, can open it too.

- Three role views of the same data:

- My health (astronaut): status, reasons, next steps, trend charts with personal baseline bands, check-ins and tests that are due, a check-in streak, and a clickable body map linking each reading to the body system and spaceflight hazard behind it.

- Crew Medical Officer: crew board, escalation queue, acknowledge, request a vision check, set follow-ups. Private check-ins open only with consent or at Orange and above, and every access is logged.

- Ground (Earth): what Earth sees after the delay, next to the live onboard status, plus a blackout switch.

- Emergency Mode: one tap on SOS (available on every screen), or holding the ESP32 button for 2 seconds, turns every screen red and shows one instruction at a time, with a CPR metronome. The medical officer takes the lead, and ground is notified with the earliest possible reply time. The crew does not wait.

- ESP32 node: detects heartbeats from an analog pulse sensor and streams heart rate to the app over USB (or Web Serial in Chrome/Edge, or Wi-Fi), shows the status on an OLED screen, sounds a buzzer at Orange, Red or SOS, and uses its button to acknowledge an alert or call SOS. The firmware never invents a reading. If the sensor stops sending for 5 seconds, the app switches to simulated values, labels them Simulated and shows a "Sensor offline" banner.

- NASA data tab: real Inspiration4 crew lab results from NASA OSDR (OSD-569 blood count, OSD-575 metabolic panel), bundled for offline use. Each crew member's three preflight samples form their personal baseline. The day-after-landing result is compared with both that baseline and the standard lab range, which shows changes that a population range would call normal. The tab also lists every rule ORBITAL uses and its source.

- Demo scenarios: a normal day; a slow warning (headaches + short sleep + rising CO2) and its resolution; a crewmate collapse; a solar storm (shelter and dose); a crew member quietly struggling (private wellbeing flag); and a sensor dropout. A mission profile switch (ISS / Moon / Mars) changes the delay and who leads.

- 16 automated tests.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Missions to Mars will face communication delays, blackouts and no evacuation. ORBITAL moves health decisions onboard, so the crew can act within minutes. The same need exists on Earth: ships, offshore platforms and remote clinics in the Gulf and elsewhere, anywhere without a doctor nearby.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It compares each person with their own baseline, not only with population averages, and shows this on real astronaut data.

- It reads body, cabin and mission data together.

- It explains every number and tells you what to do and who decides, instead of only showing data.

- It is offline-first, and escalation is designed around the communication delay to Earth.

- Its AI assistant answers only from cited documents and can never change a health status.

TOOLS

- Hardware: ESP32 dev board, analog pulse sensor, SSD1306 OLED screen, active buzzer, and the ESP32's built-in button.

- App: JavaScript. A Node.js server with no external packages (built-in web server, a live one-second data stream, local file storage). The interface is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks and nothing loaded from the internet.

- Charts and body map: drawn in SVG by our own code, with no charting library.

- Hardware link: the serialport package, or the Web Serial API in Chrome/Edge.

- Local AI (optional): Ollama running Llama 3.2 3B.

- Firmware: C++ in Arduino IDE 2 with the Espressif ESP32 core and the Adafruit SSD1306/GFX libraries. The firmware also supports a MAX30102 sensor for SpO2.

- NASA services: OSDR and the DONKI space-weather API (api.nasa.gov).

- Testing: Node.js built-in test runner.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety: no diagnosis, no medication or dosing advice. ORBITAL says "possible contributing factor", never "cause". The medical officer and mission procedures decide.

- Validity: every threshold is one of three kinds, and the app shows which. Cited: NASA-STD-3001 for cabin CO2, temperature, humidity and radiation; American Heart Association, WHO and American Diabetes Association reference ranges for blood pressure, SpO2 and glucose. Baseline: a change from the person's own preflight baseline. Team rule: set by us where no source existed, and labelled "illustrative - replace with mission medical rules".

- Honest data: every value is labelled Measured, Entered or Simulated. Open astronaut vital-sign time series are scarce, so the 14-day demo mission history is synthetic, shaped by published findings, and labelled. Cabin readings and radiation dose are simulated in the demo. Our pulse sensor measures heart rate only, so SpO2 in the demo is entered by hand or simulated, and labelled that way. The node supports a real CO2 sensor, and we deliberately do not use cheap gas sensors that cannot actually measure CO2.

- Privacy: personal check-ins are private by default. The medical officer sees status and flags; full notes open only with consent or on escalation, and every access is logged.

- Reliability: it runs without a network. If the sensor drops out, it switches to labelled simulated values within 5 seconds, and readings can still be entered by hand.

- Limitations: little human health data exists beyond low Earth orbit, so ORBITAL's Mars behaviour is design logic, not a validated result. The Inspiration4 data comes from a 3-day low-orbit flight with 4 crew and 3 preflight samples each. Hobby optical sensors are not medical devices. The emergency steps are a public basic-life-support template; real missions use approved flight medical procedures. ORBITAL is a concept demonstration, not certified medical software.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used Claude (Anthropic) to merge our team's research into one project brief, to draft the pitch script, slides and scenario animations, and to draft this submission text. SI assisted with writing and merging the code from our two early prototypes. The team reviewed and edited all SI-assisted content. The project idea, hardware build and final design decisions are our own.
